questions.q: According to the lesson, what are the three concrete outcomes an architecture review should actually reach?
options: Approved, approved with specific changes, or rejected with specific reasons
Interesting, somewhat interesting, or not interesting
Postponed, cancelled, or rescheduled
Agree to disagree, agree to agree, or no outcome needed
questions.explain: The review's purpose is a decision, not a discussion -- landing on one of these three concrete outcomes is what makes a review successful, regardless of how substantive the conversation felt.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend stating the specific decision being asked for at the start of the review ('decide whether to adopt X'), rather than an open framing ('let's discuss our options')?
options: An open framing invites an open-ended conversation with no natural endpoint, while stating the specific decision keeps the meeting oriented toward actually reaching an outcome
Stating the decision upfront is purely a formality with no effect on the meeting's outcome
Open framings always produce better technical decisions than specific ones
The starting framing has no bearing on whether the meeting reaches a decision
questions.explain: An explicit decision framing keeps the discussion anchored to a concrete endpoint; an open 'let's discuss' framing has no natural stopping point and risks ending without a real outcome.

questions.q: How should a reviewer's valid objection that falls OUTSIDE the design doc's actual scope be handled?
options: Acknowledge it as real and legitimate, capture it as a follow-up, and keep the meeting focused on today's actual decision -- without dismissing it or letting it hijack the discussion
Dismiss the objection immediately as irrelevant and move on without comment
Abandon the current review entirely to address the new concern instead
Ignore the objection completely and pretend it wasn't raised
questions.explain: The skill is routing a real but out-of-scope concern to a follow-up without either dismissing it (which feels unfair) or letting it hijack the room's limited time on today's actual decision.

questions.q: What is the honest test for whether 'let's take it offline' was the right call versus an avoidance tactic?
options: Whether the MAIN decision still got made in the meeting with only a narrow sub-question deferred, versus the entire decision being deferred under that phrase
Whether the phrase was said politely or rudely
Whether more than three people were in the meeting
'Take it offline' is always the wrong call in every situation
questions.explain: Deferring a narrow, specific detail while still reaching the main decision is legitimate; using the phrase to defer the entire decision just postpones the moment of actually deciding, which means the review didn't do its job.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a review that ends with 'great discussion, lots to think about' has failed, even if the discussion was substantive?
options: The review's actual purpose was to reach an explicit decision, not just to inform or engage people -- a substantive discussion with no concrete outcome still fails to do the review's real job
A substantive discussion always means the review succeeded regardless of outcome
Reviews should never involve any discussion at all
This outcome only counts as a failure if fewer than five people attended
questions.explain: An interesting conversation is not the point of an architecture review -- the point is a decision, and ending without one means the meeting didn't accomplish its actual purpose, however engaging it felt.
